title: CEO compensation, pay inequality, and the gender diversity of bank board of directors
abstract: Greater gender diversity on bank board of directors is associated with higher compensation inequality because CEOs at banks with more gender-diverse boards have higher base salaries. This effect disappears when women have higher representation on the board and during the financial crisis.
summary_en: Greater gender diversity on US bank boards is associated with higher CEO-pay inequality — but only up to a point. Owen and Temesváry show that CEOs at banks with more gender-diverse boards earn higher base salaries (driving wider gaps between CEO and rank-and-file pay). However, this effect disappears once female board representation crosses a higher threshold, and during the 2008 financial crisis the relationship vanishes. The result complicates simple narratives that more diversity automatically reduces inequality at the top.
data_used: Compustat ExecuComp + Federal Reserve regulatory filings on approximately 90 US bank holding companies, 1999-2015, with detailed gender composition of board of directors and full executive compensation breakdowns.
policy_relevance: Hungarian banking-sector gender-diversity policy (MNB recommendations, EU Capital Requirements Directive disclosure on board composition) typically expects diversity to reduce executive-pay extremes. The paper warns the relationship is more subtle: low diversity has different effects than high diversity, and crisis periods break the pattern. Useful framing for MNB and the Equal Treatment Authority when interpreting Hungarian bank board composition data.
